rows.en_before_tone: Write it down before you say it, to make your feelings clearer

rows.ko: 요즘 하고 싶은 일이나 진로 고민을 누군가에게 말하기 전에, 떠오르는 대로 글로 먼저 적어 보세요. 그중 꼭 전하고 싶은 문장 하나에 밑줄을 긋습니다.
rows.en: Before you talk to anyone about what you want to do or where your path is heading, write your thoughts down as they come. Then underline the one sentence you most want to get across.
rows.en_before_tone: Before telling someone about what you want to do or your worries about your path, try writing your thoughts down as they come. Then underline the one sentence you most want to share.

rows.ko: 생각이 글이 되면 막연하던 마음이 선명해져요. 정리된 한 문장이 있으면 말로 꺼낼 용기도 생깁니다.
rows.en: On paper, a fuzzy feeling turns clear. Hold one clear sentence, and you find the courage to say it out loud.
rows.en_before_tone: When thoughts become words on a page, a vague feeling becomes clearer. Having one clear sentence gives you the courage to say it out loud.

rows.ko: 새로 해보는 일 앞에서 든든한 한 사람에게 알리기
rows.en: Tell one person in your corner when you try something new
rows.en_before_tone: Tell one supportive person when you try something new

rows.ko: 이번 주 새로 시작하거나 도전하는 일이 있다면, 응원해 줄 만한 사람 한 명에게 '나 이거 해 보려고 해'라고 짧게 알려 보세요. 조언을 구하지 않아도 괜찮습니다.
rows.en: If you're starting or trying something new this week, give a quick heads-up to one person who'll cheer you on: "I'm going to give this a shot." No need to ask for advice.
rows.en_before_tone: If you're starting or trying something new this week, you might briefly tell one person who's likely to cheer you on: "I'm going to give this a try." You don't need to ask for advice.

rows.ko: 든든한 한 사람에게 시작을 알리는 것만으로도 힘이 생깁니다. 내 계획을 소리 내어 말하는 연습도 돼요.
rows.en: Telling one person in your corner that you're beginning gives you real momentum. It's also practice in saying your plans out loud.
rows.en_before_tone: Just telling one supportive person that you're starting gives you strength. It's also practice in saying your plans out loud.

rows.ko: 나를 지켜줄 문장을 소리 내어 녹음하고 다시 듣기
rows.en: Record a sentence that has your back, then play it back
rows.en_before_tone: Record a sentence that supports you, then listen back

rows.ko: 준비하다 흔들릴 때 나를 붙잡아 줄 문장 한 줄을 정해 휴대폰 음성 메모에 또박또박 녹음해 보세요. 하루 한 번 들어 보고, 믿기 어렵다면 문장을 조금 더 현실적으로 고칩니다.
rows.en: Choose one sentence that steadies you when you start to wobble during your preparations, and record it clearly as a voice memo. Listen once a day, and if it's hard to believe, tweak it until it rings true.
rows.en_before_tone: Try choosing one sentence that can steady you when you feel shaky while preparing, and record it clearly as a voice memo on your phone. Listen once a day, and if it's hard to believe, adjust it to feel a little more realistic.

rows.ko: 불안한 목소리만큼 단단한 목소리도 연습할수록 자라요. 내 목소리로 내 편을 들어 보는 경험은 다른 사람 앞에서 말할 때도 힘이 됩니다.
rows.en: A steady voice grows stronger with practice, just as an anxious one does. Take your own side, in your own voice, and you carry that strength into every room you speak in.
rows.en_before_tone: A steady voice, just like an anxious one, grows stronger the more you practice it. Taking your own side in your own voice also helps when you speak in front of others.

rows.ko: 화난 순간에 '겉감정 / 속감정 / 하고 싶던 말' 세 줄 적기
rows.en: In a moment of anger, write three lines: 'surface feeling / deeper feeling / what I wanted to say'
rows.en_before_tone: When you're angry, write three lines: 'surface feeling / deeper feeling / what I wanted to say'

rows.ko: 연애하며 화나거나 싸늘해졌던 순간 하나를 골라, 겉으로 나온 감정 한 단어, 그 아래 있던 여린 감정 한 단어, 그 감정이 하고 싶었던 말 한 문장을 적어 보세요. 속감정이 잘 안 떠오르면 '잘 모르겠음'도 충분한 답입니다.
rows.en: Pick one moment in a relationship when you got angry or went cold. Write one word for the feeling that showed on the outside, one word for the more tender feeling underneath, and one sentence for what that feeling was trying to say. If the deeper feeling won't come, "not sure" is a perfectly good answer.
rows.en_before_tone: Try picking one moment in a relationship when you felt angry or went cold. Write one word for the feeling that showed on the surface, one word for the softer feeling underneath, and one sentence for what that feeling wanted to say. If the deeper feeling doesn't come to mind, "not sure" is a perfectly good answer.

rows.ko: 겉으로 나온 화 밑에 서운함이나 불안이 숨어 있을 때가 많아요. 속마음을 찾아야 정말 하고 싶던 말을 전할 수 있습니다.
rows.en: Anger on the surface often hides hurt or worry underneath. Find what you truly feel, and you can say what you actually meant.
rows.en_before_tone: Underneath the anger that shows, hurt or worry is often hiding. Finding what you really feel inside helps you say what you truly wanted to say.

rows.ko: "왜 안 했어" 대신 "나는 이럴 때 서운했어"로 시작하기
rows.en: Start with "I felt hurt when..." instead of "Why didn't you..."

rows.ko: 서운한 일이 생기면 상대의 행동을 따지기 전에 '나는 이럴 때 서운했어'로 말을 시작해 보세요. 한 가지 장면만 짧게 말하는 것이 좋습니다.
rows.en: When something stings, open with "I felt hurt when..." before you get into what the other person did. Stick to one moment and keep it short.
rows.en_before_tone: When something hurts, try starting with "I felt hurt when..." before pointing to what the other person did. It works best to describe just one moment, briefly.

rows.ko: '왜'로 시작하는 말은 상대를 방어하게 만들기 쉽습니다. 내 마음을 주어로 말하면 상대도 귀를 열기 쉬워요.
rows.en: Opening with "why" tends to put people on the defensive. Lead with your own feelings, and the other person opens up to listen.
rows.en_before_tone: Starting with "why" tends to put the other person on the defensive. When your own feelings are the subject, they find it easier to listen.

rows.ko: 연인이 있을 때
rows.en: If you're in a relationship

rows.ko: 구체적인 한 가지를 짚어 칭찬해보기
rows.en: Compliment one specific thing
rows.en_before_tone: Give a compliment about one specific thing

rows.ko: 연인이나 요즘 알아가는 사람에게 고마웠던 행동 하나를 구체적으로 짚어 말해 보세요. '오늘 먼저 연락해 줘서 좋았어'처럼 짧아도 됩니다.
rows.en: Tell your partner, or someone you're getting to know, about one specific thing they did that you appreciated. Keep it short: "I loved that you texted me first today."
rows.en_before_tone: Try telling your partner, or someone you're getting to know, about one specific thing they did that you appreciated. It can be short, like "I loved that you texted me first today."

rows.ko: 좋은 마음도 말해야 전해집니다. 긍정적인 표현이 자주 오가면 어려운 말을 꺼낼 때도 덜 긴장돼요.
rows.en: Kind thoughts only land when you say them out loud. Let warm words flow back and forth, and the hard conversations feel far less nerve-racking.
rows.en_before_tone: Kind feelings only reach people when you say them. When warm words flow often, you'll feel less tense when hard things need to be said.

rows.ko: 불편한 마음을 푸는, 우리 집에 맞는 방식 하나 고르기
rows.en: Find the way of clearing the air that suits your family
rows.en_before_tone: Choose one way of easing tension that fits your family

rows.ko: 우리 집에서는 불편한 일이 생기면 보통 어떻게 푸는지 적고, 직접 말하기·글로 전하기·다른 가족의 도움 받기·시간 두기를 나란히 놓아 보세요. 지금 상황에 가장 맞는 방식에 별을 달고, 괜찮다면 그 방식으로 한 번 해 봅니다.
rows.en: Write down how your family usually handles it when something feels off. Then lay the options side by side: talking it out directly, putting it in writing, asking another family member for help, or giving it time. Star the one that fits best right now, and if you're ready, try it once.
rows.en_before_tone: Try writing down how your family usually handles it when something feels uncomfortable. Then list the options side by side: talking directly, writing it down, getting help from another family member, or giving it time. Star the one that fits best right now, and if you're up for it, try it once.

rows.ko: 마음을 푸는 방식은 집집마다 달라요. 우리 집에 맞는 길을 고르면 말하기의 부담이 한결 줄어듭니다.
rows.en: Every family has its own way of working through hard feelings. Choose the approach that fits yours, and speaking up feels far lighter.
rows.en_before_tone: Every family has its own way of working through hard feelings. Choosing the path that fits yours makes speaking up much less of a burden.

rows.ko: 비난 대신 내 감정을 주어로 말해보기
rows.en: Lead with your feelings instead of blame
rows.en_before_tone: Speak from your own feelings instead of blaming

rows.ko: 가족에게 불편한 점이 있을 때 '왜 맨날 그래' 대신 '나는 그 말을 들으면 좀 속상해'처럼 내 감정을 주어로 말해 보세요. 한 번에 한 가지만 전하는 것이 좋습니다.
rows.en: When something a family member does bothers you, put your own feelings front and center. Instead of "Why do you always do that?" try "It hurts a little when I hear that." Share one thing at a time.
rows.en_before_tone: When something bothers you in your family, try putting your own feelings first. Instead of "Why do you always do that?" try "I feel a bit hurt when I hear that." It's best to share just one thing at a time.

rows.ko: 탓하는 말은 대화를 다툼으로 바꾸기 쉽습니다. 내 감정을 전하면 가족도 내 마음을 알아들을 여지가 생겨요.
rows.en: Blame turns a conversation into a fight fast. Share how you feel instead, and you give your family the chance to understand where you're coming from.
rows.en_before_tone: Blaming words can easily turn a conversation into an argument. Sharing your feelings gives your family room to understand where you're coming from.

rows.ko: 욱한 순간 '멈춤 → 한 걸음 물러남' 한 번 해보기
rows.en: When you feel yourself flaring up, try 'pause, then step back' once
rows.en_before_tone: When you flare up, try 'pause, then step back' once

rows.ko: 가족과 이야기하다 화가 확 올라오면 바로 말하지 말고 잠깐 멈춘 뒤 한 걸음 물러나 숨을 길게 내쉬어 보세요. 그다음 원하는 결과를 떠올리고 할 말을 고릅니다.
rows.en: When anger surges while you're talking with family, hold your words. Pause, take a step back, and let out a long breath. Then picture the outcome you want and choose your words from there.
rows.en_before_tone: If anger suddenly rises while talking with family, try not to speak right away. Pause, take a step back, and let out a long breath. Then think about the outcome you want and choose your words.

rows.ko: 가까운 사이일수록 말이 먼저 튀어나오기 쉬워요. 한 박자 멈추면 하고 싶은 말을 내가 고를 수 있습니다.
rows.en: The closer the relationship, the faster words fly out before you think. Pause for a beat, and you take back the choice of what to say.
rows.en_before_tone: The closer the relationship, the more easily words fly out first. Pausing for a beat lets you choose what you really want to say.

rows.ko: 지금 느끼는 감정을 한 단어로 표현해보기
rows.en: Sum up how you feel in one word
rows.en_before_tone: Name what you're feeling in one word

rows.ko: 친구와 대화한 뒤나 모임에서 돌아오는 길에 지금 느끼는 감정에 한 단어로 이름을 붙여 보세요. '뿌듯함', '서운함', '지침'처럼 짧을수록 좋습니다.
rows.en: After a chat with a friend or on your way home from a get-together, give what you're feeling a one-word name. The shorter the better: "proud," "hurt," "drained."
rows.en_before_tone: After talking with a friend or on your way home from a get-together, try giving what you're feeling right now a one-word name. The shorter the better: "proud," "hurt," "drained."

rows.ko: 감정에 이름이 붙으면 막연한 기분이 조금 정리돼요. 내 마음을 먼저 알아야 다른 사람에게도 표현할 수 있습니다.
rows.en: Name a feeling, and a vague mood starts to untangle. Know what's going on inside first, and sharing it with others comes more easily.
rows.en_before_tone: Naming a feeling helps sort out a vague mood a little. Knowing your own heart first makes it easier to express it to others.

rows.ko: 전하고 싶은 말을 '속마음 / 전할 말'로 나눠 다시 쓰기
rows.en: Split what you want to say into 'what I feel / what I'll actually say'
rows.en_before_tone: Rewrite what you want to say as 'what I feel / what to share'

rows.ko: 친구에게 하고 싶은 말을 떠오르는 대로 적은 뒤, 내 감정을 쏟아 내는 부분과 상대에게 꼭 전해야 할 부분을 나눠 보세요. 전할 부분만 한두 문장으로 다듬어 둡니다.
rows.en: Write down what you want to say to a friend as it comes, then separate the venting from the parts they truly need to hear. Polish only what you'll share into a sentence or two.
rows.en_before_tone: Try writing down what you want to say to a friend as it comes, then separate the parts where you're pouring out your feelings from the parts they really need to hear. Polish just the parts to share into one or two sentences.

rows.ko: 다 털어놓는 것이 오히려 서로를 서운하게 할 때가 있어요. 꼭 필요한 말을 골라 두면 차분하게 전하기 쉽습니다.
rows.en: Pouring out everything sometimes leaves you both hurt. Choose the words that truly matter, and you say them with calm.
rows.en_before_tone: Sometimes saying everything ends up hurting both of you. Picking out the words that truly matter makes it easier to share them calmly.

rows.ko: 쌓아두지 않고 가볍게라도 표현해보기
rows.en: Speak up lightly instead of bottling it up
rows.en_before_tone: Speak up lightly instead of holding it in

rows.ko: 모임에서 메뉴나 장소, 시간에 대한 내 선호가 있다면 한 번은 가볍게 말해 보세요. '나는 이쪽이 좀 더 좋아'면 충분합니다.
rows.en: When your group makes plans and you have a preference about the food, the place, or the time, mention it casually at least once. "I'd kind of prefer this one" is all it takes.
rows.en_before_tone: If you have a preference about the menu, place, or time at a get-together, try mentioning it lightly once. "I'd kind of prefer this one" is enough.

rows.ko: 작은 의견을 삼키다 보면 서운함이 쌓이기 쉽습니다. 가볍게 자주 말하는 연습이 큰 이야기도 꺼낼 수 있는 바탕이 돼요.
rows.en: Swallow enough small opinions, and resentment quietly builds. Share little things lightly and often, and you lay the groundwork for raising the big ones.
rows.en_before_tone: Swallowing small opinions can let quiet resentment build up. Practicing light, frequent sharing builds the ground for bigger conversations too.

rows.ko: 어려운 대화를 두세 줄 대본으로 미리 써보기
rows.en: Write a two- or three-line script for a tough conversation
rows.en_before_tone: Write a short two- or three-line script for a hard conversation

rows.ko: 더치페이, 빌려준 돈, 생활비 분담처럼 꺼내기 어려운 돈 이야기 하나를 골라, 상대가 할 법한 말과 내 대답을 주고받듯 두세 줄 써 보세요. 소리 내어 읽어 보고 말투가 마음에 들 때까지 짧게 고칩니다.
rows.en: Pick one awkward money topic, like splitting the bill, money you lent, or sharing living costs. Write two or three lines of back-and-forth: what the other person might say and how you'll reply. Read it out loud and keep trimming until you like how it sounds.
rows.en_before_tone: Try picking one money conversation that's hard to bring up, like splitting the bill, money you lent, or sharing living costs. Then write two or three lines of back-and-forth: what the other person might say, and your reply. Read it aloud and tweak it until you like how it sounds.

rows.ko: 돈 이야기는 꺼내기 전이 가장 어렵습니다. 몇 줄이라도 미리 써 두면 삼키던 말이 실제로 꺼낼 수 있는 문장이 돼요.
rows.en: The hardest part of a money conversation is the moment before you start. Write even a few lines in advance, and the words you've been swallowing become sentences you can actually say.
rows.en_before_tone: Money conversations are hardest right before you start them. Writing even a few lines ahead turns the words you've been swallowing into sentences you can actually say.

rows.ko: 선택지를 두 개로 줄여 제안하기
rows.en: Narrow it down to two options
rows.en_before_tone: Suggest just two options

rows.ko: 모임이나 약속을 잡을 때 내 예산과 일정에 맞는 선택지 두 개를 먼저 제안해 보세요. '이 두 곳 중에 어때?'처럼 가볍게 말하면 됩니다.
rows.en: When you're making plans to get together, be the first to suggest two options that fit your budget and schedule. Keep it breezy: "How about one of these two?"
rows.en_before_tone: When planning a get-together or meetup, try being the first to suggest two options that fit your budget and schedule. Something light like "How about one of these two?" works.

rows.ko: 형편을 길게 설명하지 않아도 내 필요를 자연스럽게 전할 수 있어요. 먼저 제안하는 것만으로 부담스러운 지출을 줄일 수 있습니다.
rows.en: You can get your needs across without explaining your finances. Simply making the first suggestion spares you spending that feels like a stretch.
rows.en_before_tone: You can share what you need naturally without long explanations about your finances. Just suggesting first can cut down on spending that feels like a stretch.

rows.ko: "오늘 좀 지쳤어"처럼 짧게라도 감정을 말로 꺼내보기
rows.en: Put a feeling into words, even just "I'm a little worn out today"
rows.en_before_tone: Put a feeling into words, even briefly, like "I'm a bit worn out today"

rows.ko: 돈 문제로 마음이 무거운 날, 편한 사람에게 '요즘 좀 빠듯해서 신경이 쓰여'처럼 짧게 감정을 말로 꺼내 보세요. 해결책을 듣지 않아도 괜찮습니다.
rows.en: On days money worries weigh on you, tell someone you trust how you're doing, even briefly: "Money's been tight lately and it's on my mind." They don't need to fix it.
rows.en_before_tone: On a day when money worries feel heavy, try briefly telling someone you're comfortable with how you feel, like "Things are a bit tight lately and it's on my mind." You don't need to hear a solution.

rows.ko: 말하지 않은 걱정은 혼자 더 커지기 쉽습니다. 짧게라도 꺼내면 마음이 조금 가벼워지고 도움을 청할 길도 열려요.
rows.en: Unspoken worries grow in the dark. Say them out loud, even briefly, and you lighten the load and open the door to asking for help.
rows.en_before_tone: Worries left unspoken tend to grow when you're alone with them. Saying them even briefly lightens your heart a little and opens the way to asking for help.

rows.ko: 의견이 부딪친 뒤 상대 말에서 맞을 수 있는 한 조각 찾기
rows.en: After a disagreement, find one piece of their view that rings true
rows.en_before_tone: After a clash, find one piece of what they said that might be right

rows.ko: 최근 동료와 의견이 부딪친 장면 하나를 떠올려 내 생각을 '확실한 사실'과 '내 의견'으로 나눠 적어 보세요. 그다음 상대 의견에서 맞을 수도 있는 한 조각을 찾아 한 줄 씁니다.
rows.en: Think back to a recent clash with a coworker and sort your thoughts into 'hard facts' and 'my opinion.' Then find one part of their view that might hold up, and write it in a single line.
rows.en_before_tone: Try thinking of a recent moment when you clashed with a coworker, and split your thoughts into 'clear facts' and 'my opinion.' Then find one piece of their view that might be right and write it in one line.

rows.ko: 꼭 옳아야만 안심되는 마음은 오히려 쉽게 흔들려요. 한 조각을 인정해 보면 다시 마주 앉을 여유가 생깁니다.
rows.en: Needing to be right in order to feel secure actually leaves you easier to rattle. Concede one small point, and you both find room to return to the table.
rows.en_before_tone: Needing to be right in order to feel safe can actually make you easier to shake. Acknowledging one piece gives you room to sit down together again.

rows.ko: 작은 인정의 말로 관계와 분위기 데우기
rows.en: Warm the air with a small word of appreciation
rows.en_before_tone: Warm things up with a small word of appreciation

rows.ko: 부딪쳤던 동료에게 평소처럼 업무 이야기를 건네며 '정리해 주신 자료 덕분에 편했어요' 같은 작은 인정의 말을 덧붙여 보세요. 지난 일을 다시 꺼내지 않아도 괜찮습니다.
rows.en: Talk shop with the coworker you clashed with as you normally would, and slip in a little appreciation: "Your notes made this so much easier." No need to rehash what happened.
rows.en_before_tone: Try talking about work with the coworker you clashed with, just as you usually would, and add a small word of appreciation, like "The notes you put together made this much easier." You don't need to revisit what happened.

rows.ko: 갈등 뒤 어색함은 작은 말 한마디로 풀리기도 합니다. 인정의 말이 오가면 다시 함께 일할 분위기가 데워져요.
rows.en: One small comment often melts the awkwardness after a conflict. As appreciation flows both ways, working together feels warm again.
rows.en_before_tone: The awkwardness after a conflict can sometimes ease with a single small comment. When appreciation goes back and forth, the mood for working together warms up again.

rows.ko: 재직 중일 때
rows.en: If you're currently working

rows.ko: 업무 모드에서 벗어나는 전환 의식을 만들기
rows.en: Create a ritual that signals 'work mode off'
rows.en_before_tone: Create a ritual to switch out of work mode

rows.ko: 속상한 일이 있었던 날, 퇴근하면서 손을 씻거나 옷을 갈아입는 것처럼 일과 나를 떼어 놓는 동작 하나를 정해 해 보세요. 그 동작을 할 때마다 '오늘 일은 여기까지'라고 속으로 말합니다.
rows.en: On a day when something at work got to you, choose one action on your way home that separates you from the job, like washing your hands or changing your clothes. Each time you do it, tell yourself, "That's it for work today."
rows.en_before_tone: On a day when something upset you, try choosing one action that separates you from work on your way home, like washing your hands or changing your clothes. Each time you do it, tell yourself quietly, "That's it for work today."

rows.ko: 일터의 감정을 집까지 데려오면 회복할 틈이 줄어들어요. 분명한 전환 신호가 있으면 마음을 추스르기 훨씬 쉽습니다.
rows.en: Carry work feelings home, and you leave yourself less room to recover. A clear switch-off signal makes it far easier to regroup.
rows.en_before_tone: Bringing work feelings home leaves less room to recover. A clear signal to switch makes it much easier to collect yourself.

rows.ko: 재직 중일 때
rows.en: If you're currently working

rows.ko: 친구에게 건넬 말을 쓰고 한 줄을 나에게 읽기
rows.en: Write what you'd say to a friend, then read one line to yourself
rows.en_before_tone: Write what you'd tell a friend, then read one line to yourself

rows.ko: 소중한 친구가 나처럼 시험이나 지원에서 뜻대로 되지 않았다고 상상하고, 그에게 건넬 말을 몇 줄 써 보세요. 그중 한 줄을 골라 나에게 소리 내어 읽어 봅니다.
rows.en: Imagine a dear friend just missed out on an exam or an application, the same way you did. Write a few lines of what you'd say to them. Then choose one line and read it aloud to yourself.
rows.en_before_tone: Try imagining that a dear friend didn't get the result they hoped for on an exam or application, just like you. Write a few lines of what you'd say to them. Then pick one line and read it aloud to yourself.

rows.ko: 친구에게는 쉽게 건네는 다정한 말을 나에게 돌려 읽으면 자책이 조금 누그러져요. 다시 일어설 힘은 다그침보다 다정함에서 나오기 쉽습니다.
rows.en: Turn the kind words you'd easily offer a friend back toward yourself, and self-blame loosens its grip. The strength to rise again comes from kindness far more than from pushing harder.
rows.en_before_tone: Turning the kind words you'd easily give a friend back toward yourself can soften self-blame a little. The strength to get back up tends to come from kindness more than pushing yourself.

rows.ko: 막힌 목표 하나에 '갈 수 있는 길' 두 가지 적기
rows.en: Map two possible routes for one stuck goal
rows.en_before_tone: Write down two 'possible paths' for one stuck goal

rows.ko: 요즘 막혀 있다고 느끼는 목표 하나를 골라, 지금 방법 말고 그곳에 닿을 수 있는 다른 길을 두 가지만 적어 보세요. 당장 할 수 없는 길이어도 괜찮습니다.
rows.en: Pick one goal that's felt stuck lately, and list just two other ways to reach it besides what you're doing now. They don't have to be routes you can take right away.
rows.en_before_tone: Try picking one goal that feels stuck lately, and write down just two other paths that could get you there besides your current approach. It's okay if they're not paths you can take right away.

rows.ko: 희망은 덮어놓고 좋게 보는 것이 아니라 길이 있다고 믿는 거예요. 다른 길이 하나 보이면 실망에서 다시 걸음을 옮기기 쉬워집니다.
rows.en: Hope isn't blind optimism. It's believing there's a way through. Spot even one other path, and you start moving again after a setback.
rows.en_before_tone: Hope isn't about blindly looking on the bright side. It's believing there's a way. When you can see one other path, it's easier to start moving again after a disappointment.

rows.ko: 좋아하는 곡 한 곡 길이만큼 몸을 가볍게 늘여주기
rows.en: Stretch for the length of one favorite song
rows.en_before_tone: Gently stretch for the length of one favorite song

rows.ko: 뜻대로 안 된 날, 좋아하는 노래 한 곡을 틀고 그 노래가 끝날 때까지 목과 어깨, 허리를 천천히 늘여 보세요. 잘하려 애쓰지 않고 시원한 만큼만 움직입니다.
rows.en: On a day things didn't go your way, put on a song you love and slowly stretch your neck, shoulders, and lower back until it ends. Forget about doing it right. Move only as far as feels good.
rows.en_before_tone: On a day when things didn't go your way, try playing a song you love and slowly stretching your neck, shoulders, and back until it ends. There's no need to do it perfectly. Just move as much as feels good.

rows.ko: 실망은 몸에도 무겁게 남기 쉬워요. 몸을 먼저 풀어 주면 마음을 추스를 여유도 따라옵니다.
rows.en: Disappointment settles into your body, too. Loosen up physically first, and your mind follows.
rows.en_before_tone: Disappointment can sit heavily in the body too. Loosening up your body first makes room to settle your mind as well.

rows.ko: 다툴 때 내 행동을 '사실 나는 ~를 바랐다'로 다시 쓰기
rows.en: Reframe how you act in arguments as 'What I really wanted was...'
rows.en_before_tone: Rewrite your behavior in arguments as 'What I really wanted was...'

rows.ko: 다툴 때 내 행동에 붙던 이름, 예를 들어 '잔소리'나 '무심함'을 하나 적고, 그 행동으로 사실은 무엇을 바랐는지 '사실 나는 ~를 바랐다' 한 문장으로 다시 써 보세요. 행동이 남긴 영향은 그대로 두고 그 안의 바람만 꺼내 봅니다.
rows.en: Write down one label that tends to stick to how you act in arguments, like 'nagging' or 'distant.' Then rewrite what you were truly hoping for in a single sentence: "What I really wanted was..." You're not erasing the impact of what you did, just uncovering the wish underneath it.
rows.en_before_tone: Try writing down one label that tends to get attached to your behavior in arguments, like 'nagging' or 'distant.' Then rewrite what you were really hoping for in one sentence: "What I really wanted was..." Leave the impact of the behavior as it is, and just draw out the wish inside it.

rows.ko: 잔소리나 무심함 안에도 '닿고 싶다'는 바람이 있을 수 있어요. 그 바람을 알면 다툼 뒤 다시 다가갈 말이 생깁니다.
rows.en: Even nagging or distance often carries a wish to feel close. Recognize that wish, and you find the words to reach out again after a fight.
rows.en_before_tone: Even inside nagging or distance, there can be a wish to connect. Knowing that wish gives you words to reach out again after an argument.

rows.ko: 감정이 격해지면 잠깐 멈췄다 다시 이야기하기로 약속하기
rows.en: Agree to take a time-out when emotions run high
rows.en_before_tone: Agree to pause and come back when emotions run high

rows.ko: 평온할 때 연인과 '감정이 격해지면 잠깐 쉬었다가 다시 이야기하자'는 약속을 정해 보세요. 쉬는 시간과 다시 만날 때를 함께 정해 두는 것이 핵심입니다.
rows.en: While things are calm between you, make a pact with your partner: "If things get heated, let's take a short break and come back to it." The key is agreeing together on how long the break lasts and when you'll pick it back up.
rows.en_before_tone: When things are calm, try making an agreement with your partner: "If emotions get heated, let's take a short break and talk again." The key is deciding together how long the break is and when you'll come back.

rows.ko: 멈춤이 약속돼 있으면 잠시 자리를 피해도 버려진다는 느낌이 덜합니다. 서로 가라앉은 뒤에 나누는 대화가 화해로 이어지기 쉬워요.
rows.en: When you agree on a pause ahead of time, stepping away no longer feels like abandonment. Talk once you've both cooled off, and you're far more likely to make up.
rows.en_before_tone: When a pause is agreed on, stepping away for a moment feels less like being abandoned. Conversations after you've both cooled down are more likely to lead to making up.

rows.ko: 연인이 있을 때
rows.en: If you're in a relationship

rows.ko: 잠깐 눈을 감고 호흡에만 집중하는 시간을 갖기
rows.en: Close your eyes for a moment and simply breathe
rows.en_before_tone: Take a moment to close your eyes and focus only on your breath

rows.ko: 다툼 뒤 마음이 들끓을 때 편한 자리에 앉아 잠깐 눈을 감고 숨이 들어오고 나가는 것에만 주의를 두어 보세요. 생각이 떠오르면 다시 숨으로 돌아오면 됩니다.
rows.en: When you're still fuming after an argument, sit somewhere comfortable, close your eyes, and rest your attention on your breath moving in and out. If thoughts drift in, return to your breathing.
rows.en_before_tone: When your feelings are churning after an argument, try sitting somewhere comfortable, closing your eyes for a moment, and paying attention only to your breath coming in and going out. When thoughts come up, just return to your breath.

rows.ko: 몸이 진정되어야 마음도 추스를 수 있어요. 숨을 고른 뒤에는 상대의 말을 조금 더 너그럽게 들을 여지가 생깁니다.
rows.en: Calm your body first, and your mind settles with it. Once you've caught your breath, you hear the other person out with more generosity.
rows.en_before_tone: Your body needs to calm down before your heart can settle. Once you've caught your breath, there's more room to hear the other person a little more generously.

rows.ko: 지난 갈등에서 내 노력이 닿은 부분 두 가지 찾기
rows.en: Find two ways your efforts made a difference in a past conflict
rows.en_before_tone: Find two places where your efforts made a difference in a past conflict

rows.ko: 최근 가족과의 갈등과 그 결과를 한 줄로 쓰고, 결과에 내가 영향을 준 행동을 두 가지 찾아보세요. 다음에 바꿔 볼 수 있는 한 조각도 함께 적어 둡니다.
rows.en: In one line, write down a recent conflict with family and how it turned out. Then find two things you did that shaped the outcome, and note one small thing you'll try differently next time.
rows.en_before_tone: Try summing up a recent conflict with family and how it ended in one line, then find two things you did that influenced the outcome. Also jot down one small piece you could try changing next time.

rows.ko: 결과가 완벽하지 않아도 내 노력이 닿은 부분은 있어요. 그걸 확인하면 무력감 대신 다음 한 걸음이 보입니다.
rows.en: Even when things don't turn out perfectly, your efforts still count. See that clearly, and the next step comes into view instead of helplessness.
rows.en_before_tone: Even when the outcome isn't perfect, your efforts still made a difference somewhere. Seeing that helps you find the next step instead of feeling helpless.

rows.ko: 대화가 어렵다면 나란히 걷는 것부터 시작하기
rows.en: If talking is hard, start by walking side by side

rows.ko: 다툰 가족과 마주 앉아 이야기하기가 어색하다면 장보기나 동네 산책을 함께 가자고 해 보세요. 나란히 걷다 보면 굳이 지난 일을 꺼내지 않아도 됩니다.
rows.en: If sitting face to face with a family member after an argument feels awkward, invite them along to the grocery store or on a walk around the neighborhood. Walking side by side, you never have to bring up what happened.
rows.en_before_tone: If sitting face to face with a family member you argued with feels awkward, you might suggest going grocery shopping or for a walk around the neighborhood together. Walking side by side, you don't have to bring up what happened.

rows.ko: 마주 보는 대화보다 나란히 걷는 시간이 부담이 덜할 때가 있습니다. 함께 움직이는 시간이 다시 이어지는 다리가 돼요.
rows.en: Walking side by side often feels easier than a face-to-face talk. Moving together becomes the bridge that reconnects you.
rows.en_before_tone: Sometimes walking side by side feels easier than talking face to face. Time spent moving together can become a bridge back to each other.

rows.ko: 날카로운 한마디에 맞받기 전 '무슨 일 있었어?' 묻기
rows.en: Before you snap back at a sharp comment, ask "Did something happen?"
rows.en_before_tone: Before snapping back at a sharp remark, ask "Did something happen?"

rows.ko: 가족이 툭 날카롭게 말했을 때 바로 받아치거나 입을 닫는 대신, 한 박자 숨을 쉬고 '무슨 일 있었어?'라고 물어보세요. 참고 넘기라는 뜻이 아니라 엇갈림이 커지기 전에 한 번 멈춰 보는 연습입니다.
rows.en: When a family member says something sharp, skip firing back or going quiet. Take a breath and ask, "Did something happen?" This isn't about swallowing it. It's practice in hitting pause before the rift grows.
rows.en_before_tone: When a family member says something sharp, instead of snapping back or shutting down, try taking a breath and asking, "Did something happen?" This isn't about putting up with it. It's practice in pausing once before the gap grows wider.

rows.ko: 날카로운 말에 바로 맞받으면 말다툼으로 번지기 쉬워요. 속사정을 먼저 물으면 상처가 깊어지기 전에 멈출 기회가 생깁니다.
rows.en: Fire back at sharp words, and a full-blown argument follows fast. Ask what's going on first, and you give yourselves a chance to stop before anyone gets hurt more deeply.
rows.en_before_tone: Snapping back at sharp words can easily turn into an argument. Asking what's going on first gives you a chance to stop before the hurt goes deeper.

rows.ko: 최근 만남을 '한 말·그때 기분·다음에 해볼 말'로 되짚기
rows.en: Replay a recent get-together: 'what I said, how I felt, what I'd say next time'
rows.en_before_tone: Look back on a recent meetup: 'what I said, how I felt, what I'd try saying next time'

rows.ko: 어긋났던 친구와의 만남이나 대화 하나를 떠올려 내가 한 말, 그때 기분, 다음에 해 보고 싶은 말을 세 줄로 적어 보세요. 잘 안 풀린 부분보다 내가 잘한 행동 하나를 먼저 적는 것이 순서입니다.
rows.en: Think of one meetup or conversation with a friend that went sideways, and write three lines: what you said, how you felt, and what you'd like to say next time. Start with one thing you did well before you get to what didn't go smoothly.
rows.en_before_tone: Try thinking of one meetup or conversation with a friend that went sideways, and write three lines: what you said, how you felt then, and what you'd like to try saying next time. It helps to start with one thing you did well, before the parts that didn't go smoothly.

rows.ko: 천천히 되짚어 보면 잘한 점이 먼저 보이고, 아쉬운 부분은 다음에 해 볼 말의 재료가 돼요. 자책 대신 회복할 방법에 마음이 갑니다.
rows.en: Look back slowly, and you see what went right first, while the rough spots become material for next time. Instead of beating yourself up, you turn toward mending things.
rows.en_before_tone: When you look back slowly, you notice what went well first, and the regrets become material for what to say next time. Your mind turns toward ways to recover instead of self-blame.

rows.ko: 같이 웃었던 표현 다시 꺼내기
rows.en: Bring back something you used to laugh about together
rows.en_before_tone: Bring back a phrase you used to laugh about together

rows.ko: 서먹해진 친구와 함께 웃었던 표현이나 장면을 떠올려 가벼운 안부의 소재로 보내 보세요. 긴 사과나 설명 없이 짧은 메시지면 됩니다.
rows.en: Recall a phrase or moment you used to laugh about with a friend you've drifted from, and send it as a light way to check in. A short message is all it takes, with no long apology or explanation.
rows.en_before_tone: Try thinking of a phrase or moment you laughed about with a friend you've drifted from, and use it as a light way to check in. A short message is enough, no long apology or explanation needed.

rows.ko: 함께 웃었던 기억은 어색함을 녹이는 좋은 다리입니다. 가벼운 신호 하나가 다시 이어질 계기가 되기도 해요.
rows.en: Shared laughter is one of the best icebreakers there is. One light message can be exactly what brings you back in touch.
rows.en_before_tone: Memories of laughing together are a great way to melt the awkwardness. One light signal can become the start of reconnecting.

rows.ko: 서두르지 않고 음료를 음미하며 잠시 멈추기
rows.en: Slow down and savor a drink
rows.en_before_tone: Pause and savor a drink without rushing

rows.ko: 관계 때문에 속상한 날, 따뜻한 차나 좋아하는 음료를 한 잔 준비해 향과 온기를 천천히 느끼며 마셔 보세요. 마시는 동안에는 휴대폰을 내려 둡니다.
rows.en: On a day someone has left you upset, make a cup of warm tea or a drink you love, and sip it slowly, taking in its aroma and warmth. Set your phone aside while you drink.
rows.en_before_tone: On a day when a relationship has left you upset, try making a cup of warm tea or a drink you love, and sip it slowly, noticing its aroma and warmth. You can set your phone aside while you drink.

rows.ko: 마음이 복잡할 때 몸의 감각에 머물면 생각의 속도가 느려져요. 잠시 멈춰 나를 달래는 시간이 있어야 다시 다가갈 힘도 생깁니다.
rows.en: When your mind is tangled, tune in to your senses and let your racing thoughts slow down. Pause to soothe yourself, and you gather the strength to reach out again.
rows.en_before_tone: When your mind is tangled, staying with your body's senses slows down your thoughts. Taking a moment to pause and comfort yourself gives you the strength to reach out again.

rows.ko: 자책 문장을 '아쉬운 점 + 다음엔' 두 줄로 바꾸기
rows.en: Turn a self-critical thought into two lines: 'what I regret + next time'
rows.en_before_tone: Turn a self-blaming thought into two lines: 'what I regret + next time'

rows.ko: 돈을 많이 쓴 날이나 지출 계획이 틀어진 날 '난 왜 이 모양이야'가 떠오르면, 대신 '이 부분이 아쉬웠다'와 '다음엔 이렇게 해 보겠다' 두 줄을 적어 보세요. 아쉬움은 남기고 나를 깎아내리는 말만 내려놓는 연습입니다.
rows.en: On a day you overspent or your budget went off the rails, if "What's wrong with me?" pops into your head, write two lines instead: "That part didn't go great" and "Next time, I'll try this." Keep the disappointment; drop the put-downs.
rows.en_before_tone: On a day you spent a lot or your spending plan went off track, if "What's wrong with me?" pops up, try writing two lines instead: "This part was a letdown" and "Next time I'll try this." It's practice in keeping the regret while setting down the words that tear you down.

rows.ko: '아쉬웠어'와 '난 왜 이 모양이야'는 달라요. 자책을 덜어 내야 다음 지출을 조정할 힘이 남습니다.
rows.en: "That part didn't go great" and "What's wrong with me?" are worlds apart. Ease up on self-blame, and you keep the energy to adjust your spending next time.
rows.en_before_tone: "That was a letdown" and "What's wrong with me?" are not the same. Easing off self-blame leaves you the energy to adjust your next spending.

rows.ko: 미뤄둔 작은 일 목록에서 가장 작은 하나 이번 주에 끝내기
rows.en: Pick the smallest task on your put-off list and finish it this week
rows.en_before_tone: From your list of put-off tasks, finish the smallest one this week

rows.ko: 안 쓰는 구독 해지, 영수증 정리, 미뤄 둔 공과금 확인처럼 마음에 걸린 채 미뤄 둔 생활 일을 적어 보세요. 가장 작고 쉬운 하나를 골라 이번 주에 끝낸 뒤 기분을 한 줄 남깁니다.
rows.en: List the everyday chores you've been putting off that keep nagging at you, like canceling a subscription you don't use, sorting receipts, or checking a bill you've been avoiding. Pick the smallest, easiest one, get it done this week, and jot down one line about how it felt.
rows.en_before_tone: Try writing down the everyday tasks you've been putting off that keep nagging at you, like canceling an unused subscription, sorting receipts, or checking a bill you've been avoiding. Pick the smallest, easiest one, finish it this week, and write one line about how it felt.

rows.ko: 별것 아닌데 오래 미룬 일이 마음 한구석을 무겁게 차지해요. 작은 하나를 끝내면 생활을 다시 내 손에 쥔 느낌이 듭니다.
rows.en: Little tasks you've put off for ages take up a surprising amount of mental space. Cross just one off, and you feel back in control of your life.
rows.en_before_tone: Small tasks you've put off for a long time can sit heavily in a corner of your mind. Finishing just one gives you the feeling of having your life back in your hands.

rows.ko: 아무것도 안 한 시간에 '회복 시간' 이름 붙이기
rows.en: Call your do-nothing time 'recovery time'
rows.en_before_tone: Label time spent doing nothing as 'recovery time'

rows.ko: 오늘 아무것도 하지 않고 보낸 잠깐의 시간이 있었다면 그 시간에 '회복 시간'이라는 이름을 붙여 적어 보세요. 돈이 들지 않는 쉼도 회복이라는 걸 기록으로 남기는 연습입니다.
rows.en: If you spent even a few minutes today doing nothing at all, write it down and label it 'recovery time.' This is how you remind yourself, in writing, that rest that costs nothing still counts as recovery.
rows.en_before_tone: If you spent a little time today doing nothing at all, try writing it down and calling it 'recovery time.' It's a way of keeping a record that rest that costs nothing counts as recovery too.

rows.ko: 아무것도 안 한 시간도 마음이 회복되는 시간일 수 있어요. 이름을 붙이면 그 평온함을 미안함 없이 누릴 수 있습니다.
rows.en: Doing nothing is often exactly what helps you recover. Name it, and you enjoy that calm without the guilt.
rows.en_before_tone: Time spent doing nothing can also be time when your heart gets to recover. Naming it lets you enjoy that calm without feeling guilty.

rows.ko: 누구와 함께 안정을 쌓아 갈 것인가
rows.en: Who will you build stability with?

rows.ko: 최근 혼자 버티다가 누군가 곁에 있었으면 했던 순간은 어떤 장면이었나요?
rows.en: Think of a recent moment when you were getting through something alone and wished someone were there. What was happening?
rows.en_before_tone: What was a recent moment when you were getting through things alone and wished someone were by your side?

rows.ko: 마음이 놓이는 저녁을 떠올리면, 그 자리에 함께 있는 사람은 누구인가요?
rows.en: Picture an evening when you feel truly at ease. Who's there with you?
rows.en_before_tone: When you picture an evening where you feel at ease, who is there with you?

rows.ko: 요즘 내 사정을 조금 더 털어놓고 싶은 사람에게 어떤 말부터 꺼내 보고 싶나요?
rows.en: Who would you like to open up to a little more about how things have been, and what would you tell them first?
rows.en_before_tone: Is there someone you'd like to open up to a little more about how you've been? What would you want to say first?

rows.ko: 기대는 일에 에너지가 많이 드는 사람은 안정을 혼자 힘으로 만들려고 하기 쉽습니다. {{기질문장}} 그래서 다가올 해의 안정은 무엇을 더 해내느냐보다, 누구와 짐을 나눌 수 있느냐에서 시작될 수 있어요.
rows.en: Leaning on others takes a lot out of you, so you tend to build stability entirely on your own. {{기질문장}} Your stability in the year ahead begins less with getting more done and more with finding people who share the load.
rows.en_before_tone: People who find leaning on others draining often try to build stability all on their own. {{기질문장}} So stability in the year ahead may start less with how much more you can get done and more with who you can share the load with.

rows.ko: 더 높이 뛰기 위해 누구의 손을 잡을 것인가
rows.en: Whose hand will you hold to leap higher?

rows.ko: 새로운 일에 도전할 때 조언이나 도움을 구하고 싶은 사람을 떠올리면 누가 먼저 생각나나요?
rows.en: When you take on something new, who's the first person you turn to for advice or help?
rows.en_before_tone: When you take on something new, who comes to mind first as someone you'd ask for advice or help?

rows.ko: 혼자 끙끙대며 준비했던 일 가운데, 누군가와 나눴다면 달랐을 것 같은 장면은 무엇인가요?
rows.en: Think of something you prepared for alone, struggling the whole way. What would have changed if you'd shared it with someone?
rows.en_before_tone: Think of something you struggled to prepare for on your own. Which moment might have gone differently if you'd shared it with someone?

rows.ko: 한 걸음 더 나아갈 때 주변에 구체적으로 부탁하고 싶은 일은 무엇인가요?
rows.en: As you take your next step, what specific help will you ask the people around you for?
rows.en_before_tone: As you take the next step forward, what specifically would you like to ask the people around you for?

rows.ko: 기대기에 에너지가 드는 사람은 도약도 혼자 준비해서 완성된 모습만 보여 주려 하기 쉽습니다. {{기질문장}} 도움을 일찍 구할수록 준비의 무게가 줄고, 뛰어오를 힘은 오히려 커질 수 있어요.
rows.en: When relying on others doesn't come easily, you tend to prepare for a big leap alone and reveal only the finished result. {{기질문장}} Ask for help early, and the prep feels lighter while your strength to leap grows.
rows.en_before_tone: People who find leaning on others draining often prepare for a leap alone and only show the finished result. {{기질문장}} The earlier you ask for help, the lighter the preparation feels, and the more strength you may have to jump.

rows.ko: 지친 마음을 누구 곁에서 내려놓을 것인가
rows.en: Who can you let yourself be tired around?
rows.en_before_tone: Who can you set your tiredness down with?

rows.ko: 최근 가장 지쳤던 날, 그 하루를 누구에게 이야기하고 싶었나요?
rows.en: Think of your most exhausting day lately. Who did you want to tell about it?
rows.en_before_tone: On your most exhausting day recently, who did you want to tell about it?

rows.ko: 누군가 곁에 있어서 마음이 조금 풀렸던 기억은 어떤 장면인가요?
rows.en: Recall a time when simply having someone nearby made you feel lighter. What was that moment like?
rows.en_before_tone: What's a memory of a moment when having someone nearby eased your heart a little?

rows.ko: 힘들 때 받고 싶은 도움을 한 가지만 고른다면 어떤 모습의 도움인가요?
rows.en: If you could choose just one kind of support for hard times, what would it look like?
rows.en_before_tone: If you could pick just one kind of help to receive when things are hard, what would it look like?

rows.ko: 기대는 일이 어려운 사람은 지칠수록 연락을 줄이고 혼자 회복하려는 경우가 많습니다. {{기질문장}} 회복을 바란다면, 쉬는 시간만큼 마음을 내려놓을 수 있는 사람 곁에 머무는 시간도 챙겨 볼 만해요.
rows.en: If asking for support is hard, the more worn out you get, the more you go quiet and recover alone. {{기질문장}} If recovery is your wish, make time not only for rest but for being near people you can truly unwind with.
rows.en_before_tone: People who find leaning on others hard often reach out less and try to recover alone the more tired they get. {{기질문장}} If you're hoping to recover, it's worth making time to be near people you can relax with, as much as making time to rest.

rows.ko: 사랑 안에서 어떻게 기대고, 또 기댈 곳이 되어 줄 것인가
rows.en: In love, how will you lean on someone, and let them lean on you?
rows.en_before_tone: How will you lean on someone in love, and be someone they can lean on?

rows.ko: 가까운 사람에게 기대고 싶었지만 꾹 참았던 순간은 어떤 장면이었나요?
rows.en: When did you want to lean on someone close to you but hold back?
rows.en_before_tone: What was a moment when you wanted to lean on someone close but held it in?

rows.ko: 사랑받고 있다고 느끼는 순간을 떠올리면, 상대는 어떤 행동을 하고 있나요?
rows.en: Think of a moment when you feel loved. What is the other person doing?
rows.en_before_tone: When you think of a moment you feel loved, what is the other person doing?

rows.ko: 소중한 사람에게 요즘 바라는 작은 도움을 말로 옮긴다면 어떤 문장이 될까요?
rows.en: Put one small thing you'd like from someone you love right now into words. What would you say?
rows.en_before_tone: If you put into words a small kind of help you'd like from someone dear to you these days, what would you say?

rows.ko: 기대기에 에너지가 드는 사람은 사랑 안에서도 부담이 될까 봐 바라는 것을 삼키기 쉽습니다. {{기질문장}} 사랑을 바란다면, 기대는 마음을 조금씩 보여 주는 연습이 관계를 더 가깝게 만드는 열쇠가 될 수 있어요.
rows.en: Even in love, leaning on others costs you energy, so you tend to swallow what you want for fear of being a burden. {{기질문장}} If love is your wish, let someone see, little by little, that you want to lean on them. That openness is your key to growing closer.
rows.en_before_tone: People who find leaning on others draining often swallow what they want in love, worried about being a burden. {{기질문장}} If you're hoping for love, practicing showing that you want to lean on someone, little by little, could be the key to growing closer.

rows.ko: 어떤 사람들과 서로 기대며 지낼 것인가
rows.en: Who do you want in your corner, and whose corner will you be in?
rows.en_before_tone: Who will you lean on, and be leaned on by?

rows.ko: 부담 없이 도움을 주고받았던 사람과의 장면을 떠올리면, 그 관계의 어떤 점이 편했나요?
rows.en: Think of someone you could trade help with, no strings attached. What made that relationship feel so easy?
rows.en_before_tone: Think of someone you could easily give help to and receive help from. What made that relationship feel comfortable?

rows.ko: 요즘 만나고 나면 마음이 가벼워지는 사람은 누구인가요?
rows.en: Who have you been seeing lately who leaves you feeling lighter?
rows.en_before_tone: Who leaves you feeling lighter after you see them these days?

rows.ko: 조금 더 가까워지고 싶은 사람에게 먼저 건네고 싶은 말은 무엇인가요?
rows.en: Is there someone you'd like to grow closer to? What will you say to them first?
rows.en_before_tone: What would you like to say first to someone you want to get a little closer to?

rows.ko: 기대는 일이 어려운 사람에게 좋은 사람들이란 많이 아는 사람보다 편하게 기댈 수 있는 사람에 가깝습니다. {{기질문장}} 이미 곁에 있는 관계 가운데 서로 기대도 괜찮은 사람을 알아보는 것이 시작이 될 수 있어요.
rows.en: For someone who finds leaning on others hard, "good people" aren't the ones you know the most but the ones you can lean on with ease. {{기질문장}} Start by noticing who, among the people already in your life, you can comfortably lean on, and let lean on you.
rows.en_before_tone: For people who find leaning on others hard, good people aren't so much the ones you know well as the ones you can lean on comfortably. {{기질문장}} A good start may be noticing which of the people already around you it feels okay to lean on, and be leaned on by.

rows.ko: 무엇을 맡기고 숨 돌릴 틈을 만들 것인가
rows.en: What will you hand off to give yourself room to breathe?
rows.en_before_tone: What will you hand off to make room to breathe?

rows.ko: 요즘 혼자 떠안고 있는 일 가운데 누군가에게 나눠도 괜찮을 일은 무엇인가요?
rows.en: Of everything you're carrying alone right now, what could you share with someone else?
rows.en_before_tone: Of the things you're carrying alone right now, what could you share with someone?

rows.ko: 마음 편히 쉬었던 날을 떠올리면, 그날은 무엇이 달랐나요?
rows.en: Think of a day when you truly got to rest. What was different about it?
rows.en_before_tone: When you think of a day you truly rested, what was different about it?

rows.ko: 누군가에게 일을 맡길 때 마음에 걸리는 생각은 어떤 것인가요?
rows.en: When you think about handing something off, what thoughts hold you back?
rows.en_before_tone: When you hand something off to someone, what thoughts make you hesitate?

rows.ko: 기대기에 에너지가 드는 사람은 부탁하기보다 혼자 하는 쪽을 택하다가 여유를 잃기 쉽습니다. {{기질문장}} 여유는 일을 줄이는 것만큼, 맡길 수 있는 사람을 곁에 두는 데서도 생겨요.
rows.en: Asking for help takes a lot out of you, so you often do everything yourself and lose your breathing room along the way. {{기질문장}} Breathing room comes from taking things off your plate, and just as much from keeping people close you can hand things to.
rows.en_before_tone: People who find leaning on others draining often choose to do things alone rather than ask, and lose their breathing room along the way. {{기질문장}} Breathing room comes from cutting back on tasks, but also from having people you can hand things off to.

rows.ko: 누구와 함께 생활의 리듬을 지켜 갈 것인가
rows.en: Who will help you keep your daily rhythm?

rows.ko: 오래 이어 갔던 습관을 떠올리면, 그 습관을 붙잡아 준 것은 무엇이었나요?
rows.en: Think of a habit you kept up for a long time. What helped it stick?
rows.en_before_tone: Think of a habit you kept up for a long time. What helped you stick with it?

rows.ko: 산책이나 잠자리 시간처럼 누군가와 함께하면 더 쉬워질 것 같은 루틴은 무엇인가요?
rows.en: Which routine, like a walk or getting to bed on time, would be easier with someone else?
rows.en_before_tone: Which routines, like a walk or your bedtime, might feel easier if you did them with someone?

rows.ko: 생활 리듬이 흐트러질 때 편하게 알릴 수 있는 사람은 누구인가요?
rows.en: When your daily rhythm starts slipping, who can you easily tell?
rows.en_before_tone: When your daily rhythm slips, who could you easily tell?

rows.ko: 기대는 일이 어려운 사람은 생활 습관도 혼자 의지로만 지키려다 지치기 쉽습니다. {{기질문장}} 함께 걷거나 서로 잠드는 시간을 알려 주는 작은 약속이 루틴을 오래 붙잡아 주는 힘이 될 수 있어요.
rows.en: When relying on others feels hard, you tend to keep up your habits on willpower alone and wear yourself out. {{기질문장}} Small agreements, like walking together or texting each other at bedtime, keep a routine alive for the long run.
rows.en_before_tone: People who find leaning on others hard often wear themselves out trying to keep their habits on willpower alone. {{기질문장}} Small agreements, like walking together or letting each other know when you're heading to bed, can help a routine last.

rows.ko: 돈 걱정을 누구와 나누고 어떤 기준을 세울 것인가
rows.en: Who will you share money worries with, and what standards will you set?

rows.ko: 돈 문제로 혼자 계산만 거듭했던 장면을 떠올리면, 그때 가장 필요했던 것은 무엇이었나요?
rows.en: Think of a time you kept crunching the numbers alone over a money problem. What did you need most then?
rows.en_before_tone: Think of a time you kept running the numbers alone over a money problem. What did you need most then?

rows.ko: 생활비나 지출 이야기를 편하게 나눌 수 있는 사람은 누구인가요?
rows.en: Who can you talk to openly about living costs or spending?
rows.en_before_tone: Who can you talk to comfortably about living costs or spending?

rows.ko: 나에게 ‘이 정도면 넉넉하다’고 느껴지는 생활은 어떤 모습인가요?
rows.en: What does a life that feels like 'this is plenty' look like for you?
rows.en_before_tone: What does a life that feels like 'this is plenty' look like to you?

rows.ko: 기대기에 에너지가 드는 사람은 돈 고민처럼 말하기 어려운 이야기를 특히 혼자 품기 쉽습니다. {{기질문장}} 믿을 만한 사람과 생활의 기준을 함께 이야기해 보는 것만으로도 막연한 불안이 구체적인 계획으로 바뀔 수 있어요.
rows.en: If leaning on people drains you, you're especially likely to keep hard topics like money to yourself. {{기질문장}} Talk through your everyday standards with someone you trust, and vague worry turns into a concrete plan.
rows.en_before_tone: People who find leaning on others draining are especially likely to keep hard-to-say topics, like money worries, to themselves. {{기질문장}} Simply talking through your everyday standards with someone you trust can turn vague anxiety into a concrete plan.

rows.ko: 누구에게 어떤 모습으로 인정받고 싶은가
rows.en: Who do you want recognition from, and for what?

rows.ko: 애써 해낸 일을 누군가 알아봐 주었으면 했던 순간은 어떤 장면이었나요?
rows.en: When did you wish someone would notice something you worked hard to pull off?
rows.en_before_tone: What was a moment when you wished someone would notice something you worked hard to achieve?

rows.ko: 도움을 받아 해낸 일도 나의 성과라고 느껴지려면 무엇이 필요할까요?
rows.en: What would it take for wins you achieved with help to still feel like your own?
rows.en_before_tone: What would it take for things you achieved with help to feel like your own accomplishments too?

rows.ko: 내 노력을 알아봐 주었으면 하는 사람에게 어떤 말을 듣고 싶나요?
rows.en: Think of the person you hope will notice your effort. What do you want to hear from them?
rows.en_before_tone: What would you like to hear from the person you hope will notice your efforts?

rows.ko: 기대는 일이 어려운 사람은 도움 없이 해내야 제대로 인정받는다고 여기기 쉽습니다. {{기질문장}} 함께 해낸 성과도 온전히 내 것으로 받아들일 때, 인정받는 기쁨이 더 오래 머물 수 있어요.
rows.en: Leaning on others doesn't come naturally to you, so you tend to believe recognition only counts if you did it all without help. {{기질문장}} Fully own what you achieved together, and the joy of being recognized stays with you longer.
rows.en_before_tone: People who find leaning on others hard often believe they only truly earn recognition when they do it without help. {{기질문장}} When you fully accept what you achieved together as your own, the joy of recognition can stay with you longer.

rows.ko: 누구 앞에서 가장 나다운 모습이 되는가
rows.en: Who do you feel most like yourself around?

rows.ko: 꾸미지 않은 모습으로 편하게 있을 수 있는 사람과의 장면을 떠올리면, 그때 나는 어떤 모습인가요?
rows.en: Picture yourself with someone you can be completely unguarded around. Who are you in those moments?
rows.en_before_tone: Think of a time with someone you can relax around without putting on a front. What are you like in those moments?

rows.ko: 도움을 청하는 내 모습을 떠올릴 때 드는 마음은 어떤 것인가요?
rows.en: What comes up for you when you picture yourself asking for help?
rows.en_before_tone: How do you feel when you picture yourself asking for help?

rows.ko: 앞으로 조금 더 솔직하게 보여 주고 싶은 내 모습은 무엇인가요?
rows.en: What part of yourself will you show more openly from here on?
rows.en_before_tone: What part of yourself would you like to show a little more honestly from now on?

rows.ko: 기대기에 에너지가 드는 사람은 강하고 괜찮은 모습만 나답다고 여기기 쉽습니다. {{기질문장}} 기대고 싶은 마음까지 내 일부로 받아들일 때, 나다움은 더 넓고 편안해질 수 있어요.
rows.en: Because leaning on others takes real effort, you easily believe only the strong, 'I'm fine' version of you is the real you. {{기질문장}} Embrace the part of you that wants to lean on someone, and being yourself becomes roomier and more relaxed.
rows.en_before_tone: People who find leaning on others draining often believe only the strong, 'I'm fine' version of themselves is the real them. {{기질문장}} When you accept the part of you that wants to lean on others too, being yourself can feel roomier and more at ease.

rows.ko: 새로운 시작을 누구와 나누며 열 것인가
rows.en: Who do you want beside you as you begin something new?
rows.en_before_tone: Who will you share a new start with?

rows.ko: 새로운 일을 시작하려 할 때 가장 먼저 이야기하고 싶은 사람은 누구인가요?
rows.en: When you're about to start something new, who's the first person you want to tell?
rows.en_before_tone: When you're about to start something new, who do you want to tell first?

rows.ko: 혼자 시작했다가 누군가의 도움이 아쉬웠던 순간은 어떤 장면이었나요?
rows.en: When did you start something on your own and wish you'd had someone's help?
rows.en_before_tone: What was a moment when you started something alone and wished someone had helped?

rows.ko: 새 출발을 앞두고 곁의 사람에게 부탁하고 싶은 작은 도움은 무엇인가요?
rows.en: As you prepare for a fresh start, what small favor will you ask of the people close to you?
rows.en_before_tone: As you head toward a fresh start, what small help would you like to ask of the people around you?

rows.ko: 기대기에 에너지가 드는 사람은 새로운 시작도 혼자 다 준비한 뒤에야 알리려 하기 쉽습니다. {{기질문장}} 시작하는 마음을 일찍 나눌수록 낯선 길의 첫걸음이 한결 가벼워질 수 있어요.
rows.en: Relying on others costs you energy, so you tend to keep a new start to yourself until everything is ready. {{기질문장}} Share your beginning early, and your first step into the unknown feels far lighter.
rows.en_before_tone: People who find leaning on others draining often wait until everything is fully prepared before telling anyone about a new start. {{기질문장}} The earlier you share that you're starting, the lighter the first step on an unfamiliar path can feel.

rows.ko: 무엇이 있으면 마음을 놓을 수 있는가
rows.en: What would it take for you to feel at ease?
rows.en_before_tone: What would help you feel at ease?

rows.ko: 최근 걱정이 잦아들고 마음이 놓였던 순간은 어떤 장면이었나요?
rows.en: Think of a recent moment when your worries settled and you could breathe easy. What was happening?
rows.en_before_tone: What was a recent moment when your worries quieted down and you felt at ease?

rows.ko: 불안할 때 가장 먼저 확인하게 되는 것은 무엇인가요?
rows.en: When anxiety hits, what's the first thing you find yourself checking?
rows.en_before_tone: When you feel anxious, what's the first thing you check?

rows.ko: 흔들리는 날에도 변하지 않고 곁에 있는 것을 떠올리면 무엇이 생각나나요?
rows.en: What stays by your side, steady and unchanged, even on shaky days?
rows.en_before_tone: When you think of something that stays by your side, unchanged, even on shaky days, what comes to mind?

rows.ko: 믿기에 에너지가 드는 사람은 안정을 바랄수록 확인하고 대비하는 일에 힘을 많이 쓰기 쉽습니다. {{기질문장}} 이미 나를 받치고 있는 것들을 알아보는 일이 안정으로 가는 첫걸음이 될 수 있어요.
rows.en: Trusting takes a lot out of you, and the more you crave stability, the more energy you pour into double-checking and bracing for what's next. {{기질문장}} Notice what's already holding you up. That is your first step toward stability.
rows.en_before_tone: People who find trusting draining often spend a lot of energy checking and preparing, especially when they're hoping for stability. {{기질문장}} Noticing the things already holding you up can be the first step toward stability.

rows.ko: 확신이 다 서지 않아도 내디딜 수 있는 한 걸음은 무엇인가
rows.en: What step can you take even before you feel completely sure?
rows.en_before_tone: What step can you take even before you feel fully sure?

rows.ko: 해 보고 싶었지만 ‘아직은 아니야’ 하며 미뤄 둔 일은 무엇인가요?
rows.en: What have you wanted to try but kept putting off, telling yourself 'not yet'?
rows.en_before_tone: What's something you've wanted to try but put off, telling yourself 'not yet'?

rows.ko: 결과를 알 수 없는 일을 시작했을 때 마음을 붙잡아 준 것은 무엇이었나요?
rows.en: When you started something without knowing how it would turn out, what kept you grounded?
rows.en_before_tone: When you started something with an uncertain outcome, what kept you steady?

rows.ko: 새 도전이 계획대로 되지 않아도 괜찮다고 느끼려면 어떤 준비가 있으면 좋을까요?
rows.en: What safety net would help you feel okay even if a new challenge doesn't go as planned?
rows.en_before_tone: What kind of preparation would help you feel okay even if a new challenge doesn't go as planned?

rows.ko: 믿기에 에너지가 드는 사람은 모든 것이 확실해질 때까지 출발을 미루기 쉽습니다. {{기질문장}} 도약을 바란다면, 완벽한 확신 대신 돌아올 자리를 마련해 두는 것이 열쇠가 될 수 있어요.
rows.en: When trust doesn't come easily, you tend to hold off on starting until everything feels certain. {{기질문장}} If a leap is your wish, the key isn't perfect certainty. Secure a place to come back to, and then jump.
rows.en_before_tone: People who find trusting draining often put off starting until everything feels certain. {{기질문장}} If you're hoping to leap, the key may be setting up a place to come back to instead of waiting for perfect certainty.

rows.ko: 무엇을 믿고 긴장을 내려놓을 것인가
rows.en: What will you trust so you can let your guard down?
rows.en_before_tone: What will you trust so you can let go of tension?

rows.ko: 몸은 쉬고 있는데 마음은 계속 긴장하고 있던 순간은 어떤 장면이었나요?
rows.en: When was your body resting while your mind just wouldn't switch off?
rows.en_before_tone: What was a moment when your body was resting but your mind stayed tense?

rows.ko: ‘이제 괜찮다’고 느끼며 깊이 쉬었던 기억을 떠올리면, 그때 무엇이 달랐나요?
rows.en: Think of a time you rested deeply, feeling 'I'm okay now.' What was different then?

rows.ko: 걱정을 잠시 내려놓기 위해 나에게 해 주고 싶은 말은 무엇인가요?
rows.en: What will you tell yourself so you can set your worries down for a while?
rows.en_before_tone: What would you like to tell yourself so you can set your worries down for a while?

rows.ko: 믿기에 에너지가 드는 사람은 쉬는 동안에도 다음 걱정을 미리 챙기느라 회복이 더디기 쉽습니다. {{기질문장}} 회복은 할 일을 멈추는 것만큼, 잠시 마음을 놓아도 된다고 스스로 허락하는 데서 시작돼요.
rows.en: If trusting drains you, you often spend your downtime preparing for the next worry, and your recovery slows. {{기질문장}} Recovery begins not only when you step away from your to-do list, but when you give yourself permission to relax.
rows.en_before_tone: People who find trusting draining often keep getting ready for the next worry even while resting, so recovery can be slow. {{기질문장}} Recovery starts not only with pausing your to-do list, but also with giving yourself permission to relax for a while.

rows.ko: 사랑 안에서 무엇을 믿고 마음을 열 것인가
rows.en: In love, what will you trust so you can open your heart?
rows.en_before_tone: What will you trust in love, so you can open your heart?

rows.ko: 가까운 사람의 답장이 늦을 때 마음속에 떠오르는 생각은 어떤 것인가요?
rows.en: When someone close to you is slow to text back, what thoughts start running through your head?
rows.en_before_tone: When someone close takes a while to reply, what thoughts come up for you?

rows.ko: 사랑받고 있다고 믿게 해 주는 작은 행동은 무엇인가요?
rows.en: What little things help you believe you're loved?
rows.en_before_tone: What small actions help you believe you're loved?

rows.ko: 관계 안에서 확인하고 싶은 마음이 들 때 나를 안심시키는 방법은 무엇인가요?
rows.en: When you crave reassurance in a relationship, how do you soothe yourself?
rows.en_before_tone: When you feel the urge to seek reassurance in a relationship, how do you calm yourself?

rows.ko: 믿기에 에너지가 드는 사람은 사랑 안에서도 상대의 마음을 거듭 확인하고 싶어지기 쉽습니다. {{기질문장}} 확인보다 이미 받은 다정함을 기억하는 연습이 사랑을 더 편안하게 만들 수 있어요.
rows.en: Even in love, trusting takes effort, so you often want to check, again and again, how your partner feels. {{기질문장}} Instead of checking, practice remembering the kindness you've already received, and love feels more relaxed.
rows.en_before_tone: People who find trusting draining often want to keep checking how the other person feels, even in love. {{기질문장}} Making a habit of remembering the kindness you've already received, rather than checking, can help love feel more at ease.

rows.ko: 어떤 사람 곁에서 마음을 놓을 수 있는가
rows.en: Who do you feel at ease around?

rows.ko: 처음에는 조심스러웠지만 점점 편해진 사람을 떠올리면, 어떤 순간에 마음이 열렸나요?
rows.en: Think of someone you were wary of at first but slowly grew comfortable with. When did you start to open up?
rows.en_before_tone: Think of someone you were cautious with at first but grew comfortable around. When did you start to open up?

rows.ko: 함께 있을 때 긴장이 풀리는 사람들에게는 어떤 공통점이 있나요?
rows.en: What do the people you can relax around have in common?
rows.en_before_tone: What do the people you relax around have in common?

rows.ko: 조금 더 믿어 보고 싶은 관계는 누구와의 관계인가요?
rows.en: Which relationship would you like to put a little more trust in?
rows.en_before_tone: Which relationship would you like to trust a little more?

rows.ko: 믿기에 에너지가 드는 사람은 새로운 관계에 마음을 여는 데 시간이 필요합니다. {{기질문장}} 좋은 사람들과의 인연은 천천히 믿음을 쌓아도 괜찮은 관계에서 자라는 경우가 많아요.
rows.en: Trust takes energy for you, so you naturally need time before opening up to new people. {{기질문장}} Your best connections grow in relationships where you're free to build trust slowly.
rows.en_before_tone: People who find trusting draining need time to open up to new relationships. {{기질문장}} Bonds with good people often grow in relationships where it's okay to build trust slowly.

rows.ko: 모든 것을 대비하지 않아도 괜찮은 틈은 어디인가
rows.en: Where can you let go of planning for everything?
rows.en_before_tone: Where is it okay not to prepare for everything?

rows.ko: 계획이 틀어졌는데도 생각보다 괜찮았던 날은 어떤 장면이었나요?
rows.en: When did your plans fall apart, yet things turned out better than you expected?
rows.en_before_tone: What was a day when your plans fell apart but things turned out better than you expected?

rows.ko: 미리 걱정하느라 즐기지 못했던 순간을 떠올리면, 그때 마음은 어디에 가 있었나요?
rows.en: Think of a moment you couldn't enjoy because you were busy worrying ahead. Where was your mind?
rows.en_before_tone: Think of a moment you couldn't enjoy because you were worrying about what might happen. Where was your mind then?

rows.ko: 조금 느슨하게 두어도 괜찮을 일은 무엇인가요?
rows.en: What could you loosen your grip on a little?
rows.en_before_tone: What could you afford to leave a little loose?

rows.ko: 믿기에 에너지가 드는 사람은 만일을 대비하느라 여유가 있어야 할 자리까지 걱정으로 채우기 쉽습니다. {{기질문장}} 여유는 모든 경우를 준비했을 때가 아니라, 준비하지 않은 부분을 믿고 내버려 둘 때 생기기도 해요.
rows.en: For you, trusting feels draining, and bracing for every 'what if' fills even the space meant for breathing room with worry. {{기질문장}} Breathing room comes not from preparing for everything, but from trusting the parts you haven't prepared for and letting them be.
rows.en_before_tone: People who find trusting draining often fill even the spaces meant for breathing room with worry, preparing for every 'what if.' {{기질문장}} Breathing room sometimes comes not when you've prepared for every case, but when you trust the unprepared parts and let them be.

rows.ko: 어떤 루틴이 마음을 놓게 해 주는가
rows.en: What routines help you settle?
rows.en_before_tone: Which routines help you feel at ease?

rows.ko: 하루를 마칠 때 마음이 차분해지는 습관은 어떤 것인가요?
rows.en: What habit helps you wind down at the end of the day?
rows.en_before_tone: What habit helps you feel calm at the end of the day?

rows.ko: 잠들기 전 걱정이 이어지는 밤, 생각을 내려놓는 데 도움이 됐던 것은 무엇인가요?
rows.en: On nights when worries keep you up, what helps you let go of your thoughts?
rows.en_before_tone: On nights when worries keep going before sleep, what has helped you let go of your thoughts?

rows.ko: 매일 같은 시간에 해서 하루의 기둥이 되어 줄 작은 습관은 무엇일까요?
rows.en: What small habit, done at the same time every day, could anchor your day?
rows.en_before_tone: What small habit, done at the same time each day, could become an anchor for your day?

rows.ko: 믿기에 에너지가 드는 사람에게는 예측할 수 있는 하루의 흐름이 든든한 버팀목이 될 수 있습니다. {{기질문장}} 매일 반복되는 작은 루틴은 생활을 정돈해 줄 뿐 아니라, 흔들리는 날에도 돌아올 기준이 되어 줘요.
rows.en: If trusting takes a lot out of you, a predictable daily flow becomes a steadfast source of support. {{기질문장}} Small daily routines keep your life in order, and on shaky days they give you something steady to come back to.
rows.en_before_tone: For people who find trusting draining, a predictable flow to the day can be a steady support. {{기질문장}} Small daily routines don't just bring order to life. They also give you something to come back to on shaky days.

rows.ko: 마음이 놓이는 나만의 생활 기준은 무엇인가
rows.en: What's your own everyday standard for feeling secure?
rows.en_before_tone: What everyday standard helps you feel at ease?

rows.ko: 돈 걱정이 가장 커졌던 순간을 떠올리면, 그때 무엇이 가장 불안했나요?
rows.en: Think back to when your money worries were at their worst. What scared you most then?
rows.en_before_tone: Think of when your money worries were at their biggest. What made you most anxious then?

rows.ko: 통장을 볼 때 마음이 편해지는 상태를 말로 옮기면 어떤 모습인가요?
rows.en: When you check your bank account, what would it need to show for you to feel at ease?
rows.en_before_tone: When you check your bank account, what would it need to look like for you to feel at ease?

rows.ko: 비상금이나 고정 지출처럼 마음이 놓이게 해 줄 생활의 기준은 무엇일까요?
rows.en: What everyday ground rules, like an emergency fund or a clear view of your fixed costs, would let you breathe easier?
rows.en_before_tone: What everyday standards, like an emergency fund or fixed expenses, could help you feel at ease?

rows.ko: 믿기에 에너지가 드는 사람은 돈이 늘어도 ‘아직 부족하다’는 불안이 쉽게 가라앉지 않을 수 있습니다. {{기질문장}} 막연한 목표 대신 마음이 놓이는 생활의 기준을 구체적으로 정해 두면, 경제적 여유를 느끼는 순간이 더 분명해져요.
rows.en: When trust takes effort, that nagging 'it's still not enough' feeling lingers no matter how much your savings grow. {{기질문장}} Trade the vague goal for a concrete everyday baseline that puts your mind at ease, and you start to recognize financial ease when it arrives.
rows.en_before_tone: For people who find trusting draining, the anxious sense of 'it's still not enough' may not settle easily, even as their money grows. {{기질문장}} Setting a concrete everyday standard that helps you feel at ease, instead of a vague goal, can make moments of financial ease clearer.

rows.ko: 남의 평가 없이도 믿을 수 있는 나의 노력은 무엇인가
rows.en: Which of your efforts can you believe in, even without anyone's praise?
rows.en_before_tone: Which of your efforts can you trust, even without others' praise?

rows.ko: 칭찬을 들었는데도 마음이 놓이지 않았던 순간은 어떤 장면이었나요?
rows.en: Recall a time you were praised but still couldn't relax. What was happening?
rows.en_before_tone: What was a moment when you were praised but still didn't feel at ease?

rows.ko: 누가 알아주지 않아도 스스로 잘했다고 느꼈던 일은 무엇인가요?
rows.en: What's something you know you did well, even though nobody noticed?
rows.en_before_tone: What's something you felt you did well, even though no one noticed?

rows.ko: 내가 해낸 일을 스스로 확인할 수 있는 방법은 무엇일까요?
rows.en: How will you keep track of your own wins, on your own terms?
rows.en_before_tone: How could you confirm for yourself what you've accomplished?

rows.ko: 믿기에 에너지가 드는 사람은 인정을 받아도 그 말을 온전히 믿기까지 시간이 걸리기 쉽습니다. {{기질문장}} 바깥의 평가와 함께 스스로 확인할 수 있는 기록을 쌓아 갈 때, 인정이 마음에 더 오래 남을 수 있어요.
rows.en: If trust doesn't come easily, even sincere praise takes a while to sink in. {{기질문장}} Keep your own record of what you've done alongside other people's feedback, and recognition finally stays with you.
rows.en_before_tone: People who find trusting draining often take a while to fully believe praise, even when they receive it. {{기질문장}} When you build up your own record alongside outside feedback, recognition can stay with you longer.

rows.ko: 흔들려도 믿을 수 있는 나의 중심은 무엇인가
rows.en: What steadfast core of yours can you count on, even when you're shaken?
rows.en_before_tone: What center in you can you trust, even when you waver?

rows.ko: 남의 반응을 살피느라 내 선택을 바꿨던 순간은 어떤 장면이었나요?
rows.en: Recall a time you changed course because you were worried how others would react.
rows.en_before_tone: What was a moment when you changed your choice because you were watching how others would react?

rows.ko: 어떤 상황에서도 지키고 싶은 나만의 기준은 무엇인가요?
rows.en: What personal rule will you hold on to, whatever happens?
rows.en_before_tone: What's a personal standard you want to keep, no matter the situation?

rows.ko: 내가 나를 믿는다고 느꼈던 순간을 떠올리면, 그때 나는 무엇을 하고 있었나요?
rows.en: Think of a moment you truly trusted yourself. What were you doing?
rows.en_before_tone: Think of a moment you felt you trusted yourself. What were you doing then?

rows.ko: 믿기에 에너지가 드는 사람은 바깥의 반응에 따라 나에 대한 믿음도 함께 흔들리기 쉽습니다. {{기질문장}} 나다움은 흔들리지 않는 것이 아니라, 흔들린 뒤에도 돌아갈 나의 기준을 아는 데서 단단해져요.
rows.en: For those who struggle to trust, self-belief rises and falls with other people's reactions. {{기질문장}} Being yourself doesn't mean never wobbling. You grow steadfast by knowing exactly which values to return to once you do.
rows.en_before_tone: People who find trusting draining often find their belief in themselves shifting along with other people's reactions. {{기질문장}} Being yourself grows steady not by never wavering, but by knowing your own standard to return to after you do.

rows.ko: 모든 것이 확실하지 않아도 무엇을 믿고 시작할 것인가
rows.en: You don't have every answer yet. What will you trust as you begin?
rows.en_before_tone: Even if not everything is certain, what will you trust as you begin?

rows.ko: 시작하고 싶었지만 확신이 서지 않아 미뤄 둔 일은 무엇인가요?
rows.en: What have you wanted to start but kept putting off because you didn't feel sure?
rows.en_before_tone: What's something you wanted to start but put off because you didn't feel sure?

rows.ko: 낯선 일을 처음 시작했을 때 나를 버티게 해 준 것은 무엇이었나요?
rows.en: The first time you tried something unfamiliar, what kept you going?
rows.en_before_tone: When you first started something unfamiliar, what helped you keep going?

rows.ko: 새로운 시작이 생각과 다르게 흘러가도 돌아올 수 있는 자리는 어디인가요?
rows.en: If a new start doesn't unfold the way you pictured, where can you come home to?
rows.en_before_tone: If a new start turns out differently than you imagined, where can you come back to?

rows.ko: 믿기에 에너지가 드는 사람은 새 출발 앞에서 앞일이 다 보일 때까지 기다리기 쉽습니다. {{기질문장}} 새로운 시작을 바란다면, 확신보다 이미 나를 받쳐 주는 것을 알아보는 일이 첫걸음을 도울 수 있어요.
rows.en: When trust is hard, you tend to wait at the starting line until you can see the whole road ahead. {{기질문장}} If a fresh start is your wish, don't wait to feel certain. Notice what already holds you up, and let that carry your first step.
rows.en_before_tone: People who find trusting draining often wait, at the edge of a fresh start, until they can see everything ahead. {{기질문장}} If you're hoping for a new start, noticing what already supports you, rather than waiting for certainty, can help with the first step.

rows.ko: 안정을 지키기 위해 어디에 선을 그을 것인가
rows.en: Where will you draw the line to keep your life steady?
rows.en_before_tone: Where will you draw the line to protect your stability?

rows.ko: 부탁을 들어준 뒤 마음이 오래 불편했던 순간은 어떤 장면이었나요?
rows.en: Think of a time you said yes to a favor and felt uneasy about it long afterward.
rows.en_before_tone: What was a moment when you agreed to a favor and felt uneasy about it for a long time afterward?

rows.ko: 내 일상이 흔들리지 않으려면 지켜야 할 시간이나 공간은 무엇인가요?
rows.en: What time or space do you need to protect to keep your days on an even keel?
rows.en_before_tone: What time or space do you need to protect so your daily life stays steady?

rows.ko: 정중하게 사양해 보고 싶은 일이 있다면 어떤 말로 전하고 싶나요?
rows.en: Is there something you'd like to politely turn down? How will you put it?
rows.en_before_tone: If there's something you'd like to politely decline, how would you want to say it?

rows.ko: 선 지키기에 에너지가 드는 사람은 남의 부탁을 받아 주다가 정작 내 일상의 안정을 잃기 쉽습니다. {{기질문장}} 안정을 바란다면, 무엇을 더 할지보다 무엇을 받아들이지 않을지 정하는 것이 먼저일 수 있어요.
rows.en: If holding boundaries wears you out, saying yes to everyone else quietly costs you the stability of your own routine. {{기질문장}} If stability is what you want, start by deciding what you won't take on, before you think about what to add.
rows.en_before_tone: People who find holding boundaries draining often lose the stability of their own daily life while saying yes to others' requests. {{기질문장}} If you're hoping for stability, deciding what you won't take on may come before deciding what more to do.

rows.ko: 도약을 위해 무엇을 거절하고 무엇에 집중할 것인가
rows.en: What will you say no to, and what will you go all in on, to make your leap?
rows.en_before_tone: What will you say no to, and what will you focus on, to make your leap?

rows.ko: 남의 일을 돕느라 내 계획이 뒤로 밀렸던 장면을 떠올리면, 그때 미뤄진 것은 무엇이었나요?
rows.en: When did your own plans last get pushed aside while you helped with someone else's work? What got put on hold?
rows.en_before_tone: Think of a time your own plans got pushed back because you were helping with someone else's work. What got put off then?

rows.ko: 가장 집중하고 싶은 일 하나를 고른다면 무엇인가요?
rows.en: If you could pick just one thing to focus on, what would it be?
rows.en_before_tone: If you could pick just one thing to focus on most, what would it be?

rows.ko: 그 일을 지키기 위해 줄이거나 사양하고 싶은 것은 무엇인가요?
rows.en: To protect that, what will you cut back on or turn down?
rows.en_before_tone: To protect that, what would you like to cut back on or decline?

rows.ko: 선 지키기에 에너지가 드는 사람은 모든 요청에 응하다 보면 도약에 쓸 시간과 힘이 흩어지기 쉽습니다. {{기질문장}} 한 곳에 힘을 모으려면, 거절도 앞으로 나아가는 선택이라는 감각이 열쇠가 될 수 있어요.
rows.en: When boundaries are hard to hold, saying yes to every request scatters the time and energy your big leap needs. {{기질문장}} Gather your strength in one place, and remember: every no you say is also a step forward.
rows.en_before_tone: People who find holding boundaries draining can scatter the time and energy they'd need for a leap by saying yes to every request. {{기질문장}} To gather your energy in one place, the key may be seeing that saying no is also a choice that moves you forward.

rows.ko: 회복을 위해 지켜야 할 나의 경계는 어디인가
rows.en: What boundaries do you need so you can actually recover?
rows.en_before_tone: What boundaries do you need to protect your recovery?

rows.ko: 쉬려고 했는데 연락이나 부탁 때문에 쉬지 못했던 날은 어떤 장면이었나요?
rows.en: Recall a day you meant to rest but couldn't because of messages or requests.
rows.en_before_tone: What was a day when you meant to rest but couldn't, because of messages or requests?

rows.ko: 온전히 나만을 위해 쓰고 싶은 시간은 언제인가요?
rows.en: When do you want time that's entirely your own?
rows.en_before_tone: When do you want time that's fully just for you?

rows.ko: 지친 날 ‘오늘은 어렵다’고 말한다면 어떤 표현이 가장 편할까요?
rows.en: On a tired day, what's the easiest way for you to say 'Today doesn't work for me'?
rows.en_before_tone: On a tired day, what would be the most comfortable way to say 'Today doesn't work for me'?

rows.ko: 선 지키기에 에너지가 드는 사람은 지쳐 있어도 남의 요청을 먼저 챙기다 회복할 틈을 놓치기 쉽습니다. {{기질문장}} 회복을 바란다면, 쉬는 시간에도 경계를 세워 두는 것이 가장 실질적인 돌봄이 될 수 있어요.
rows.en: Setting limits takes a lot out of you. Even when you're running on empty, you put others' requests first and miss your chance to recharge. {{기질문장}} If recovery is your wish, draw a firm line around your downtime. That is the most practical self-care there is.
rows.en_before_tone: People who find holding boundaries draining often put others' requests first even when they're worn out, and miss the chance to recover. {{기질문장}} If you're hoping to recover, keeping boundaries around your rest time can be the most practical way to care for yourself.

rows.ko: 사랑 안에서 나를 지키는 선은 어디인가
rows.en: In love, where's the line that keeps you, you?
rows.en_before_tone: Where is the line that protects you in love?

rows.ko: 가까운 사람에게 맞추다가 나를 잃은 것 같았던 순간은 어떤 장면이었나요?
rows.en: Think of a time you bent so far for someone close that you felt you'd lost yourself.
rows.en_before_tone: What was a moment when you went along with someone close so much that you felt you'd lost yourself?

rows.ko: 사랑하는 사이에서도 꼭 지키고 싶은 나만의 시간이나 공간은 무엇인가요?
rows.en: Even in a loving relationship, what time or space do you want to keep just for you?
rows.en_before_tone: Even in a loving relationship, what time or space of your own do you most want to keep?

rows.ko: 소중한 사람에게 서운하지 않게 ‘이건 어려워’라고 말한다면 어떤 문장이 좋을까요?
rows.en: How could you tell someone you care about 'This is hard for me' without hurting their feelings?
rows.en_before_tone: If you wanted to tell someone dear, without hurting them, 'This is hard for me,' what sentence would work well?

rows.ko: 선 지키기에 에너지가 드는 사람은 가까운 관계일수록 거절이 상처가 될까 봐 망설이기 쉽습니다. {{기질문장}} 건강한 선은 거리를 만드는 벽이 아니라, 오래 곁에 머물 수 있게 해 주는 울타리에 가까워요.
rows.en: If boundaries don't come easily, the closer the relationship, the more you hesitate to say no for fear of hurting someone. {{기질문장}} A healthy boundary isn't a wall that pushes people away. Think of it as a garden fence: it lets you stay close for the long haul.
rows.en_before_tone: People who find holding boundaries draining often hesitate to say no, especially in close relationships, worried it might hurt. {{기질문장}} A healthy boundary isn't a wall that creates distance. It's more like a fence that lets you stay close for a long time.

rows.ko: 누구와 가까이, 누구와는 적당히 지낼 것인가
rows.en: Who will you keep close, and who at a comfortable distance?
rows.en_before_tone: Who will you stay close to, and who will you keep at a comfortable distance?

rows.ko: 만나고 나면 유난히 지치는 관계를 떠올리면, 어떤 순간에 힘이 빠지나요?
rows.en: Which relationship leaves you most drained? When does your energy dip?
rows.en_before_tone: Think of a relationship that leaves you especially drained. At what moments does your energy drop?

rows.ko: 거절해도 관계가 흔들리지 않았던 사람은 누구인가요?
rows.en: Who's someone you've said no to without it hurting the relationship?
rows.en_before_tone: Who is someone you've said no to without it shaking the relationship?

rows.ko: 시간을 더 쓰고 싶은 관계와 조금 덜 쓰고 싶은 관계는 무엇인가요?
rows.en: Which relationships deserve more of your time, and which a little less?
rows.en_before_tone: Which relationships would you like to spend more time on, and which a little less?

rows.ko: 선 지키기에 에너지가 드는 사람은 모든 관계에 같은 힘을 쓰다가 정작 좋은 사람들에게 쓸 마음이 남지 않기 쉽습니다. {{기질문장}} 관계마다 거리를 다르게 두는 것이 소중한 사람들과 더 깊어지는 방법이 될 수 있어요.
rows.en: When drawing lines feels draining, you end up giving every relationship the same energy, with little left for the people who matter most. {{기질문장}} Keep different distances with different people. That is how you grow closer to the kindred spirits you treasure.
rows.en_before_tone: People who find holding boundaries draining often spend the same energy on every relationship, leaving little heart for the good people in their lives. {{기질문장}} Keeping different distances with different people can be a way to grow closer to the ones who matter.

rows.ko: 여유를 위해 무엇을 내 몫에서 덜어 낼 것인가
rows.en: What will you take off your plate to give yourself breathing room?
rows.en_before_tone: What will you take off your plate to make room to breathe?

rows.ko: ‘이건 내 일이 아닌데’ 싶으면서도 맡았던 일은 무엇이었나요?
rows.en: What's a task you took on even while thinking, 'This isn't really my job'?

rows.ko: 일정표에 아무것도 없는 시간을 떠올리면, 그 시간에 하고 싶은 일은 무엇인가요?
rows.en: Picture a stretch of time with nothing on your calendar. What would you love to do with it?
rows.en_before_tone: When you picture time with nothing on your schedule, what would you like to do with it?

rows.ko: 한 번쯤 내려놓아도 괜찮을 역할은 무엇인가요?
rows.en: What role could you let go of, just this once?
rows.en_before_tone: What role would it be okay to set down for once?

rows.ko: 선 지키기에 에너지가 드는 사람은 거절하지 못한 일들로 일정이 채워져 여유가 사라지기 쉽습니다. {{기질문장}} 여유는 시간이 남을 때 생기기보다, 내 몫과 남의 몫을 나누는 선에서 만들어져요.
rows.en: If saying no is hard for you, your calendar fills up with things you couldn't turn down until there's no breathing room left. {{기질문장}} Breathing room doesn't simply appear when you have spare time. You create it by separating what's yours to carry from what belongs to someone else.
rows.en_before_tone: People who find holding boundaries draining often see their schedule fill up with things they couldn't say no to, and their breathing room disappears. {{기질문장}} Breathing room comes less from having spare time and more from drawing a line between what's yours to carry and what's someone else's.

rows.ko: 내 생활 리듬을 지키기 위해 무엇에 선을 그을 것인가
rows.en: What will you draw the line at to protect your daily rhythm?
rows.en_before_tone: What will you draw a line around to protect your daily rhythm?

rows.ko: 늦은 연락이나 갑작스러운 약속 때문에 생활 리듬이 흐트러졌던 날은 어떤 장면이었나요?
rows.en: Recall a day when late-night messages or last-minute plans threw off your routine.
rows.en_before_tone: What was a day when late messages or last-minute plans threw off your daily rhythm?

rows.ko: 잠드는 시간이나 식사 시간처럼 꼭 지키고 싶은 생활의 기준은 무엇인가요?
rows.en: What daily basics, like your bedtime or mealtimes, matter most to you?
rows.en_before_tone: What daily standards, like your bedtime or mealtimes, do you most want to keep?
